passage: Week one. In the Class 10 physics test, Sachin knew every answer. He left two blank on purpose. When the boys joked about the "topper nerd" in the next row, he laughed along and felt sick. Week two. His teacher sent him to a weekend science camp in the city. There he met Bidisha, who argued with him for an hour about whether time really exists. Neither of them had to pretend. On the bus home, Sachin realised he hadn't felt that light in months. Week three. He got a plain, middling mark in the art project and waited for the old panic. It didn't come. His mentor at the camp had told him, "You don't need to be top in everything. Be curious." He showed his mother the lopsided pot and they both laughed.

qa.q: Who did Sachin argue with about whether time really exists?
qa.a: Bidisha, at the weekend science camp.

qa.q: Why did Sachin feel sick while laughing along with the boys?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and false, because he was hiding his ability to belong and pretending went against who he is.

qa.q: What turning point eased the pressure on Sachin?
qa.a: Meeting like-minded Bidisha at the camp, and a mentor telling him he doesn't need to be top in everything.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have experienced the argument with Sachin?
qa.a: Bidisha probably enjoyed it too, finding someone who could match that curiosity without either of them pretending.

grounding: It shows a gifted teen who hides his ability to belong and feels pressure to be top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be average sometimes.

passage: "You think you're the first one to feel this, Preeti?" Aparna Masi put down her knitting. "When I was your age, I was the girl who always topped. Every exam, every year. Teachers read my essays aloud. And do you know what I did at lunch? Ate alone in the library. I told myself it was because I liked books. Partly true. Mostly, I didn't know how to talk to the others. Then one exam I came fourth, and I cried so hard I threw up. Fourth! My science teacher found me. She said, 'Aparna, you are allowed to be ordinary on a Tuesday.' I laughed for the first time that week. She took me to the chess club, where no one cared about my rank. So if you get a B on this test, beta, the world keeps turning."

qa.q: Where did Aparna eat lunch as a teenager?
qa.a: Alone in the library.

qa.q: What does crying so hard after coming fourth show about how Aparna felt then?
qa.a: It shows she felt crushed, as if every result had to be top and anything less was failure.

qa.q: Which moment helped teenage Aparna the most?
qa.a: Her teacher told her she was allowed to be ordinary and took her to the chess club, where no one cared about her rank.

qa.q: How might Aparna's science teacher have seen her crying over coming fourth?
qa.a: The teacher seems to have seen a lonely girl crushed by her own pressure, not a failure, and wanted her to know ordinary was allowed.

grounding: An elder recalls being a gifted teen who felt out of step and pressured to top everything, relieved by a mentor, a like-minded club and permission to be ordinary.

passage: In their small town near Pala, everyone knew Thomas had topped the district exams. At cricket, the boys called him "Professor," not kindly. So in class he started leaving easy questions blank, hoping to seem normal. At home he redid every test paper, terrified that a single 98 would mean he was slipping. He felt alone in both places. Vidya Teacher, who ran the town library's evening astronomy group, stopped him one day. "Come on Saturday. Four others your age are building a telescope." He went. They argued about moons till nine at night, and nobody called him Professor. Walking home, Vidya said, "You know you're allowed a B sometimes?" Thomas laughed, and something in his chest let go.

qa.q: What did the boys at cricket call Thomas?
qa.a: They called him "Professor," not kindly.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel about his results before joining the astronomy group?
qa.a: He felt terrified and alone, worried a single 98 meant he was slipping, while also hiding his ability to fit in.

qa.q: What helped ease the strain on Thomas?
qa.a: Meeting like-minded peers in the astronomy group and hearing from a mentor that he was allowed a B sometimes.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to see Thomas?
qa.a: She sees a bright boy who is lonely and under too much pressure, and wants him to have friends and room to be ordinary.

grounding: Shows a gifted teenager out of step with peers, hiding ability and afraid of not being top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be average.

passage: In Gothenburg, Beatriz, fourteen, had started getting a few quiz answers wrong on purpose. When she scored full marks, the girls at her table went quiet and stopped inviting her to the café after school. At home she cried over a B in handball class, as if it proved something. Her maths teacher noticed the pattern and introduced her to Anders, who ran a maths circle on Thursday evenings at the university. The first night, a boy argued with her about a proof for twenty minutes, and she walked out grinning. At dinner her mother said, "A B in handball is just fine. You don't have to be first in everything." Beatriz stopped faking wrong answers. She had somewhere she belonged now.

qa.q: Who ran the maths circle Beatriz joined?
qa.a: Anders ran the maths circle on Thursday evenings at the university.

qa.q: How did Beatriz feel when her friends stopped inviting her after full marks?
qa.a: She felt lonely and left out, which is why she began getting answers wrong on purpose.

qa.q: What two things relieved the pressure on Beatriz?
qa.a: Finding peers who enjoyed arguing about proofs, and her mother telling her that a B in handball is fine.

qa.q: How might Beatriz's mother feel seeing her daughter cry over a handball grade?
qa.a: She may feel worried and sad that Beatriz believes she must be first in everything, which is why she reassures her.

grounding: Shows a gifted teenager hiding ability to belong and fearing any result that is not top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be average.

passage: At two in the morning, the house master at the residential school, Suraj Sir, found Ira in the common room redoing a lab report. "It got 18 out of 20," she said, not looking up. "I lost two marks." Her eyes were red. Ira, sixteen, had few friends in the hostel; the others found her intense. Suraj Sir sat down. "Ira, you are allowed to be ordinary sometimes. Eighteen is fine. Sleep is not optional." The next week, he introduced her to three seniors preparing for the science olympiad, who met in the library after dinner. At the first meeting she laughed at a physics joke only they got. That night she slept straight through.

qa.q: What mark did Ira get on the lab report?
qa.a: She got 18 out of 20.

qa.q: How was Ira feeling at two in the morning?
qa.a: She was anxious and upset about losing two marks, redoing the report with red eyes.

qa.q: What did Suraj Sir do that relieved Ira's strain?
qa.a: He gave her permission to be ordinary, insisted she sleep and introduced her to like-minded seniors.

qa.q: How might the olympiad seniors see Ira after the first meeting?
qa.a: They may see her as one of them, someone who laughs at the same physics jokes, not as too intense.

grounding: Shows a gifted teenager who feels out of step and that every result must be top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be ordinary.

passage:
Dear Bidisha Didi,
You asked in your last email how Class 10 is going. Honestly? Lonely. At lunch everyone talks about the same show, and when I mention the black hole paper I read, they look at me like I'm from another planet. So I've started pretending I didn't understand the maths homework either, just to fit in.
And then there's the other thing. Papa pins every rank card on the fridge. When I came second in chemistry, I couldn't sleep.
But something good happened. Ms Rao sent me to the district astronomy club. There are kids there who argue about telescopes for hours. I felt normal for the first time in months.
And Ms Rao said something I keep repeating: "You're allowed to be average at some things." It felt like putting down a school bag.
Write back soon,
Sangeeta

qa.q: Where did Ms Rao send Sangeeta?
qa.a: To the district astronomy club.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel at lunch with classmates?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt lonely and out of step, so much so that pretending not to understand the homework seemed the only way to fit in.

qa.q: What helped relieve the pressure, and why?
qa.a: Finding like-minded kids at the astronomy club and a mentor's permission to be average sometimes, which eased the need to be top in everything.

qa.q: How might Bidisha Didi feel reading this email?
qa.a: Bidisha Didi might feel concerned about the loneliness and sleepless night, and relieved that Sangeeta has found a place to feel normal.

grounding: Sangeeta feels out of step, hides ability to belong and feels every result must be top, until like-minded peers and a mentor's permission to be average relieve the strain.
